newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Kookmin Bank targets NZ niche.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kookmin Bank targets NZ niche.

text.p: South Korean retail banking giant Kookmin Bank has set its sights on a narrow target market of around 20,000 migrants in New Zealand, and hundreds of small businesses linked to this community, the managers of its newly-authorised Auckland branch said on Wednesday.

After a three-month study by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Kookmin was formally accepted as the country's 19th registered bank on Monday and is now preparing to convert its representative office into a branch within a few months.
Manager Kim Sang-jin told Reuters the pursuit of a migrant community as a client base was a new development for the bank.

Although other Korean competitors have made inroads in the United States by serving the expatriate market, Kookmin has taken an alternative tack there and is concentrating its North American expansion ambitions on wholesale and merchant banking.
However, Kim said an application has been submitted for a retail operation in Buenos Aires where the the bank hopes to use an Auckland-style approach to Korean migrants in Argentina.

Korean immigration into New Zealand went through a boom phase in the early 1990s, after the government relaxed its laws for a time. In addition to an estimated 15,000 resident Koreans, Kookmin believes there are another 4,000 students at various
colleges. They are also part of the target market.
"We're really here to fill a niche for the retail market," Kim said, noting that the bank would offer types of banking product that were attuned to national preferences.
"One difference with Oriental-style banking is the passbook system...most Korean migrants feel they are uncomfortable with the statement-based approach of New Zealand banks," he added.

Kookmin will replicate a Korean "look" for customers, while offering NZ dollar-based deposits and lending including business financing. It will also offer a link back to won-denominated assets in Korea for individuals or businesses seeking to use
these to secure loans.
This type of translation system is also widely exploited by other Korean banks in the United States, Kim noted.
Instalment-based savings plans, with fixed rates for one to five years, are other products appealing to Korean customers but seldom seen in New Zealand retail banks, he added.

On the trade front, where Korea was New Zealand's fifth biggest trade partner in 1996 with a total volume of about US$1.4 billion, Kookmin sees opportunities mainly in the import/export sector rather than supporting big corporate deals.

Deputy representative Kim Jeong-sool said the bank believes there are about 650 Korean-operated businesses in the country, spanning export sectors including timber and related products, agricultural products like deer velvet and wool, and fisheries.
Historically most bilateral trade has been carried out in US dollars, but the Kookmin managers saw ongoing finance reforms and liberalisation in South Korea helping change this pattern.
Past uncertainties around the won's value on foreign exchange markets also present Kookmin another opportunity, linked to New Zealand's popularity with Korean tourists.
Kim Sang-jin predicted the bank would be active in wholesale won/kiwi dollar foreign exchange, servicing the bureaux de change market with more dynamic rates than currently prevail.
About 127,000 Korean tourists came to New Zealand in 1996, the fifth largest number of arrivals by nationality.
Kookmin has also geared up a treasury operation in the 15-person branch to service its larger customers.
It will in part target new migrants in New Zealand's "business investor" category -- required to bring assets into the country as part of their immigration qualification.
